title: Ndakina: Maine Before Europeans
short_description: The Abenaki perspective on pre-contact period land claims.
credit:
The Ndakina, the W8banaki Nation's territory (Le Ndakina. Territoire des W8banaki), 2023
Produced by the Musée des Abénakis, Odanak, Québec

views.interpretive_text:
This map was created by the museum of the Odanak Abenaki Council, of Québec, Canada. W8banaki Nation occupies a vast territory, which it calls the "Ndakina" ("our territory"). The Ndakina stretches from New England's Atlantic coast to the St. Lawrence River to the north and the Richelieu River to the west. For thousands of years, the Abenaki and their ancestors traveled the Ndakina as semi-nomads. They traveled from the southern Appalachians to the St. Lawrence Valley further north by way of three major routes.

Abenaki Ndakina lies between the boreal forest of the Atikamekw Nehirowisiwok and lnnu to the north, the lands of the Kanien'keha:ka (Mohawk) to the west and those of the Wolastoqiyik (Maliseet), the Mi'kmaq and the Passamaquoddy to the east. The Odanak Abenaki Council of Québec and the Maliseet, the Mi'kmaq and Passamaquoddy of Maine are all members of the Waponahki (Wabanaki Confederacy).

views.title: Naming the landscape
views.interpretive_text: The Odanak Abenaki Council’s map of Ndakina shows the names of well known Maine landmark in the Abenaki language. In the cases of Mount Kineo and Kathadin (Ktaden), Euro-Americans have adopted the Abenaki names. In the case of Moosehead Lake- Euro-Americans have adopted a translation of the Abenaki Moz8depinebes.

views.title: Borders? What Borders?
views.interpretive_text: Looking closely at the map of Ndakina, you will notice that the Abenaki claimed territory crosses multiple state boundaries as well as the US/Canadian border. Here we can see portions of Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, and Québec.

title: Dividing Up the Continent
short_description: See how Europeans envisioned the northeast in the 17th century.
credit:
Le Canada ou Nouvelle France, 1656
Published by Pierre Mariette (1569-1657), Paris, France
Cartographer: Nicolas Sanson (1600-1667)

views.interpretive_text:
This map shows the initial segmentation of eastern North America by European powers. The Maine landscape is split between France and England.  The colonies of Dutch New Holland (Nouveau Pays Bas), English Virginia (Virginie), French Florida (Floride Francois) and Spanish Florida (La Floride Espagnole) are also shown.

You might notice that this map is in the French language. This is for two primary reasons.  First, in the 1600s, French transitioned from a regional vernacular into the dominant lingua franca of European intellectualism.  It was expected that all educated people could speak, read and write French.  Second, it was recognized that the French were the best cartographers (mapmakers) in the 17th century (1600s).

views.title: The Dividing Line
views.interpretive_text: We all learn in school that the State of Maine was split from Massachusetts in 1820, did you know that in the 17th century, the land that would become Maine was claimed by two different countries? During the colonization of North America, Britain and France fought with each other and with Native American nations for control of the continent. This map shows the French crowns version of where the dividing line existed between New England (Nouvelle Angleterre), outlined in yellow, and New France (le Canada or Nouvelle France), outlined in green.

views.title: Acknowledging the Native Presence on the Landscape.
views.interpretive_text: During the 17th century, the Native peoples of Maine were still a dominant force on the landscape. This map lists several Wabanaki names recorded as the French heard them. Highlighted here from south to north, we can see familiar Wabanaki names Abnaquiois (Abenaki), and Quinibequi R. (Kennebec River). We also see the names used by the French for Native nations used by the French. During the 17th century, the French revered to the Passamaquoddy as the Etechemins and the Mi’kmaqs as the Souriquois.

title: The English View
short_description: Explore North America's transition from Dutch to English dominance.
credit:
A Map of New England and New York, 1676
Published by Basset and Chiswell, London, England
Cartographer: John Speed (1542-1629)

views.caption: 1676 Default Map
views.interpretive_text:
One of the few English maps of New England produced before 1700, this map depicts the territories claimed by the British after the capture of New Amsterdam (present-day Manhattan) in 1664. The pivotal event dramatically altered the political landscape of North America, ending Dutch control of the region and ushering in an era of English colonial dominance.

Featuring the East Coast from Maryland to the French possessions in Canada, including all of New England. One of the earliest maps to use the names New York, New Larsey (New Jersey), and Boston to identify colonies.

views.title: The Maine Coast
views.caption: The Maine Coast
views.interpretive_text:
Map detail showing the coastline of Maine from the Passataquack (Piscataquis River) at the modern southern border to the mouth of the Penobscot River near Castine, and all lands north to Quebec along the St. Lawrence River. New Scotland, later Nova Scotia, was settled in 1629 and encompassed all lands from Newfoundland to New England.

In addition to anglicizing Dutch and Indigenous place names on earlier maps, this map excludes Indigenous Homelands and representations of the Native people who lived in those territories.

views.title: The Fur Trade
views.caption: The Fur Trade
views.interpretive_text: Much of the area is depicted as a vast, untouched wilderness, with illustrations of animals important to European markets and the fur trade. These include bear, beaver, egret, elk, ermine, fox, and otter.

views.title: Inaccuracies
views.caption: Inaccuracies
views.interpretive_text: This map contains errors and other geographical inaccuracies typical of 17th century maps. Examples include exaggerating the St. Lawrence River, omitting Lake Ontario, and placing Lake Champlain, labeled here as the Lake of the Irocoisiensis, representing the Five Nations of the Iroquois Confederacy, too far east of its actual location.

title: The Colonies at War
short_description: Take a look at Maine and the Northeast during the French and Indian War.
credit:
Partie Orientale de la Nouvelle France ou du Canada (Translation: Eastern part of New France or Canada), 1755
Published by Heritiers de Homan, Nuremberg, Germany
Cartographer: Jacques-Nicolas Bellin (1703-1772)

views.interpretive_text:
Dated 1755, this map is a German copy of a French cartographer’s map of the northeastern most region of the North American continent.  In 1755, the lands that would become the American northeast and the Canadian Provinces of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia were embroiled in the French and Indian War. 

The French and Indian War was fought between the years 1754 and 1763, comprising the armies of Great Britain and France, along with their respective Native American and First Nations allies as they fought for control of North America. The war was the North American theater of the Seven Years’ War, a conflict that is often considered the first major multi-national conflict, more recently referred to as World War Zero in historical texts.

views.title: Fortified Landscape
views.interpretive_text: The colonies of New England and New France were a war zone in 1755.  The cartographers have chosen to show the locations of all the forts and fortified settlements to inform the viewer of the extent of military presence on the landscape. Both French and British forts are noted, however  there is no clear designation as to which is which. Several forts are listed under a name that was antiquated by 1755.  For example, Fort Halifax in Winslow, Maine is listed on this map as Fort Taconic (Taconnet), the name of a 17th century trading post at the site. Additionally, a Fort Kook is shown in modern Augusta.  This is likely a reference to the Cushnoc Trading Post (ca. 1628-1661. An accurate 1755 map should have shown Fort Western which was built in 1754, in modern Augusta.

views.title: Fur, Fish, and Faith
views.interpretive_text: It is an often-cited refrain that New France was founded on the three Fs: Fur, Fish, and Faith.  The French sent missionaries to convert the Native Americans to Catholicism. The missions and colonies were bankrolled by the European markets in fur and fish.  This map shows the importance of fish to the North American economy by illustrating George’s Bank (Banc de St. George) and the Scotian Shelf (Les Banc d’Accadie on l’on la peche) where fishing was done.

views.title: The Native Presence Continues
views.interpretive_text: One of the points of ‘l’Intelligence des affaires et de l'Estate présent en Amérique’ to be communicated was in regard to the local Native American population. While what would become Maine was peppered with European forts and towns in 1755, the tribal name Abenakis is boldly written across the landscape between the Androscoggin (R. Sagadehoc)  and Penobscot Rivers. The persistence of Native influence is demonstrated by the fact that toponyms Penobscot, Kennebec (R. Kinibeki), and many others remain in our lexicon to this day.

title: A Feel for Maine
short_description: See how Maine was envisioned in America’s first atlas.
credit:
The Province of Maine from the Best Authorities, 1795
Published by Mathew Carey (1760-1839), Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
Cartographer: John Reid (c. 1764-1828)

views.interpretive_text:
Maine begins to take a recognizable shape in this map.

As the title suggests, Massachusetts claimed Maine as a territory or “province” with northern borders defined only by mountains that had yet to be formally surveyed.

This map was originally created to be included in America’s first atlas and is more artistic than factual. The map maker communicates a feel for Maine, but does not document many of the existing towns and roads.

views.title: King's Highway to Route 1
views.interpretive_text:
The first public roads in Maine were rutted dirt trails wide enough for a horse and cart. The roads were so rough that in 1653, the Massachusetts commissioners ordered a road built. Colonists called it the “King's Highway.”

As seen in this map, by 1795, the road extended to Pownalboro, the location of the colony’s northernmost courthouse. After the American Revolution, Massachusetts changed the name to the “Post Road.”

This road is the precursor to U.S. Route 1 in Maine.

views.title: A Border of Mountains
views.interpretive_text:
The map maker drew mountains, making them: “The Boundary Line Between the United States and the British Possessions by Treaty 1783.”

When this map was created, 12 years after the American Revolution, the international border between the American-held Province of Maine and British Canada remained in dispute.

views.title: Forts for Trade and Protection
views.interpretive_text:
Although several forts from previous wars were still standing in 1795, the mapmaker chose to only identify the location of two: Fort Halifax in Winslow and Fort Western in present-day Augusta. Both stood on the Kennebec River. 

The first forts in Maine were built to trade with the local Indigenous people. After hostilities broke out over settler claims to Indigenous land, the region descended into nearly 100 years of intermittent war. The forts afforded protection.

title: Lotteries and Land Grants
short_description: Dividing up the province of Maine.
credit:
Maine entworfen von D. F. Sotzmann (Translation: Maine drawn by D. F. Sotzmann), 1798
Published by Carl Ernst Bohn (1749-1827), Hamburg
Cartographer: Daniel Friedrich Sotzmann (1754-1840)

views.caption: 1798 Default Map
views.interpretive_text:
In this map, we begin to see many present-day Maine towns, land grants, and five of today’s sixteen counties arranged in vertical stripes.

Post roads are beginning to connect the towns, most of which are formed along waterways. The northern region is still largely unmapped.

This map was produced by Germans and includes translated names.

views.title: An Unpopular Lottery
views.caption: An Unpopular Lottery
views.interpretive_text:
This numbered grid shows lots of “Lottery Land” split between Hancock and Washington counties, which are not in the same location as the present-day counties.

Massachusetts distributed these lands after the Revolutionary War to pay off their war debts. Sixty pounds bought a ticket that guaranteed a lot of land, but acreage and quality were up to chance.

Much of the lottery land was not claimed, since the lands were inferior to areas that had already been settled. There were 2,760 lots, but only 437 tickets were sold.

views.title: Wabanaki Territory
views.caption: Wabanaki Territory
views.interpretive_text:
This strip of land along the Penobscot River is labeled “Land reserved for the Indians.”

It is smaller than the adjacent land sold to a single man, William Bingham, a wealthy Philadelphia banker.

North of here, along the border of Hancock and Washington counties, there is a place labeled “Indian Village.” These are the only two mentions of Indigenous land ownership within the borders of Maine.

views.title: German Mapmaking
views.interpretive_text:
If you look closely, you will notice that the legend and some place names are written in both English and German. 

This map was prepared for Christopher Ebeling, a German scholar who studied America and created an atlas. Ebeling commissioned Daniel Friedrich Sotzmann to engrave a set of maps, including this one. 

Soltzmann’s maps were packed with information, showing stagecoach roads, post roads, terrain, waterways, and border lines. Note that rivers are marked “Fl.” for the German “fluss.

title: Tour of Discoveries
short_description: Follow the State of Maine’s first expedition into Maine’s uncharted northern woods.
credit:
Map of the District of Maine from the Latest and Best Authorities, 1815
Published by Cummings & Hilliard, Boston, Massachusetts
Cartographer: Moses Greenleaf Esq. (1777-1834)

views.interpretive_text:
In 1820, the District of Maine became an independent state. Much of northern and eastern Maine remained uncharted wilderness. Maine’s first Governor, William King, hired Major Joseph Treat to survey northeastern Maine. Treat enlisted the help of John Neptune, lieutenant governor of the Penobscot tribe, to guide him across the Wabanaki homeland. Treat depended on Neptune’s knowledge of the land and traditional skills to navigate deep into Maine where roads were few and waterways acted as highways. 

Treat carried this map and made notations of their journey in red ink often documenting where Native peoples lived in 1820.

views.title: Launching the “Tour of Discoveries”
views.interpretive_text: To begin the journey, in what Joseph Treat called their “tour of discoveries,” Treat, fellow surveyor, Jacob Holyoke, and their Penobscot guide, John Neptune began paddling birch bark canoes loaded with supplies up the Penobscot River from Bangor. Treat placed red dots to mark their route.

views.title: The Tip of Present-Day Maine
views.interpretive_text:
Treat’s journey was the first expedition representing the State of Maine to travel to the upper Saint John Valley. The region was largely out of reach for people and goods traveling from Maine’s population center in the south. But for locals traveling west to east, including Maliseet families as well as British and French traders and settlers, the Saint John Valley was a major trade route. 

The map notes where “French and Indian Villages” were located as well as how many families

views.title: Penobscot Treaty Lands
views.interpretive_text:
Treat noted in red the location of several “Indian Townships” that they encountered on their journey. In his journal, Treat described these as “pleasant situations.”

The two Indian Townships noted here were each six square miles and had been reserved for the Penobscot by an 1818 treaty with Massachusetts.

title: The Disputed Territory
short_description: Learn how Maine's undefined northern border nearly led to war between the United States and the United Kingdom.
credit:
Maine and the Disputed Territory, 1839
Published by The Family Magazine. J. A. James & Co., Cincinnati, Ohio

views.caption: 1839 Default Map
views.interpretive_text: For decades, the boundary between Maine and Canada was poorly defined. In the 1820s, tensions escalated as the United States and Great Britain disagreed over the exact location. This dispute became known as the “Northeastern Boundary Controversy” and is often called the “Aroostook War” because it brought the two nations close to open conflict. Ultimately, the crisis was peacefully resolved with a treaty signed in 1843, which officially defined the boundary and gave Maine its recognizable shape.

views.title: The Proposed Boundaries
views.caption: The Proposed Boundaries
views.interpretive_text:
The green line shows the boundary claimed by the United States under the 1783 Treaty of Paris, which ended the American Revolution.

The red line indicates the boundary proposed by Great Britain, which at the time controlled Canada.

The blue line shows the boundary proposed by the King of the Netherlands, who was requested to arbitrate the land dispute.

views.title: The Aroostook War
views.caption: The Disputed Territory
views.interpretive_text:
The yellow area shows the disputed territory.

With both nations claiming the territory, the United States sought to retain the region for its valuable timber and natural resources, while Great Britain considered it essential for maintaining military and transportation routes between New Brunswick and Quebec. As tensions grew among local residents—many of them lumbermen—who accused one another of trespassing and illegal logging, what began as a dispute over resources and jurisdiction quickly escalated into an international crisis.

Known variously as the Aroostook War, the Madawaska War, the Pork and Beans War, and the Lumberjack War, the bloodless border dispute lasted from 1838 to 1839. Despite the absence of major combat, the conflict saw the mobilization of local militias, the deployment of troops, and the taking of prisoners by both American and British authorities, bringing the two nations to the brink of war before a diplomatic resolution was reached.

views.title: The Shape of Maine
views.interpretive_text:
In 1842, United States Secretary of State Daniel Webster and British diplomat Lord Ashburton negotiated the treaty, resolving border disputes between the U.S. and British North American colonies. 

Webster and Ashburton agreed on a division of the disputed territory in Maine, giving 7,015 square miles to the United States and 5,012 to Great Britain. Other treaty provisions included open navigation in several bodies of water and the allowance for an estimated 12,000 runaway slaves to remain free in Canada.

The U.S. Government paid Maine and Massachusetts $150,000 each for the loss of land and for expenses incurred during the truce period.

title: Transporting Goods
short_description: Explore Maine’s first railroads and their proponents’ vision for the future.
credit:
Colton’s Railroad & Township Map of the State of Maine, 1855
Published by Joseph H. Colton (1800-1893), New York, and Charles C. Hall (1822-1881), Maine

views.interpretive_text:
This map shows the extent of Maine’s railroad lines in 1855. The state’s first railroad began operating in 1836. Ten years later, railroad operators began laying rail lines throughout Maine. 

This map documents that by 1855 several major lines had been laid and shows many more proposed railroads. At this time, railroads focused on moving goods and raw materials, such as farm produce, some terminating in interior towns like Skowhegan and Buckfield.

views.title: Plans for the Future
views.interpretive_text:
Looking closely at the map, you can see where existing railroads ran and where they were proposed. The map doesn’t show every “Common” vehicle road in Maine, but larger ones are documented.

The map also notes that italicized towns had post offices and railroad depots.

views.title: Maine’s First Railroad
views.interpretive_text: The state’s first railroad began construction in Old Town, Penobscot County, in 1833. It opened for operation in 1836 and ran 12 miles. It was named the Bangor & Piscataquis Canal & Rail-Road. This railroad hauled lumber from a sawmill at Old Town for transfer to ships at Bangor.

views.title: Portland becomes Montreal’s Winter Port
views.interpretive_text:
Maine’s first international railway opened in July 1853, linking Portland to Montreal, Canada. The Atlantic & St. Lawrence began construction in 1846 after advocates for Portland beat out those in Boston to become Canada’s ice-free winter port. This development brought jobs, taxes, and other revenues to Maine. 

The line was leased to the Grand Trunk Railroad soon after it was completed.

title: Let’s Ride the Train!
short_description: Before cars dominated the roads, railways took people where they wanted to go.
credit:
Map of the State of Maine Showing Railroads, Towns, Plantations and Wild Lands, 1900
Published by George F. Cram (1842-1928), Chicago, Illinois
Created by G. F. Cram, E. C. Farrington and F. E. Oak

views.interpretive_text:
This 1900 map excludes roads to focus on Maine’s 24 railroads that extended 1,911 miles and  dominated Maine’s landscape. While some lines focused on moving products, passenger travel had become a priority with many railroad lines terminating in tourist areas. 

Some of the railroad lines are patterned or color-coded to mark different company’s rails. Others appear as black lines.

views.title: Tourism Driven
views.interpretive_text: As tourism became increasingly important to the Maine economy, railroad companies adapted to meet travelers’ demands. One example is the Maine Central Railroad. Although the line mostly carried products and raw materials, one of its branches ended at a steam ferry landing,  taking tourists to Bar Harbor on Mount Desert Island.

views.title: Serving Industry
views.interpretive_text:
Some rail lines, like the Bangor & Aroostook Railroad, terminate at remote industrial sites such as the Katahdin Iron Works. Workers mined iron ore one mile west of the company’s furnace that refined the ore into pig iron.

The first trip from the Bangor and Katahdin Iron Works Railway in 1882 made this product available to national markets. The Bangor & Aroostook purchased this small railroad in 1891.

views.title: Public Transportation
views.interpretive_text: In the years before widespread use of automobiles, electric trolleys glided along street railways linking Maine’s many rural towns to larger ones. In 1900, Maine had 21 street railways servicing 43 large towns as well as the smaller villages in between. This system, with 268 miles of streetcar lines, helped workers commute, families visit one another, and delivered tourists to their destinations.

title: Take the Road
short_description: Look where cars could easily travel before the interstate system.
credit:
State Highway Commission Map of Maine, 1935, reprinted 1936
Published by the Maine State Highway Commission, Augusta, Maine

views.interpretive_text:
At the turn of the 20th century, Maine roads were sand, rock, and clay that reportedly became like glue in the rain. 

Maine began developing a state highway system in 1901. By 1935, the state had about 23,000 miles of highway and 4,200 bridges. The speed limit was 35 miles an hour in “open country”. At the time, there were no interstates in America. It took over 18 hours to travel in a car from Kittery, the southernmost point of Maine, to Fort Kent at Maine’s northern tip.

views.title: Extent of U.S. Rt. 1
views.interpretive_text: In 1935, U.S. Route 1 extended over 2300 miles. It began in Miami, Florida, and ended at Fort Kent, Maine. The road was first designated as a federal road in 1926 and was improved in phases over time. The Maine section of Rt. 1 was 563.3 miles long.

views.title: Capitol Region
views.interpretive_text:
This map shows only numbered state roads. Smaller connecting roads between towns do not appear on the map. 

Most of the state roads in the capitol region around Augusta (indicated in red) were hard roads made of concrete, asphalt, or treated gravel. Many others (appearing as thick black) were still unimproved gravel roads. The portions outlined in black, but not filled in, and roads marked as thin black lines remained dirt roads.

views.title: Prioritizing Southern Maine
views.interpretive_text: The red lines on the map represent hard roads that have been improved to facilitate automobile travel. These are concentrated in the southern region of the state, the population center of Maine. U.S. Route 1 snakes along the Downeast coastline before heading north.  A few hard roads extend into New Hampshire and Canada.

title: Greetings From Maine
short_description: Maine is more than "Vacationland." Learn about the state's recreational and industrial attractions.
credit:
“Greetings From Maine” Postcard, circa 1960
Published by Tichnor Brothers Inc., Boston, Massachusetts

views.interpretive_text:
Throughout the 20th century, Maine increasingly identified itself as America’s “Vacationland,” even adopting the slogan for its license plates in 1936. As highway systems expanded, pictorial maps became popular, promoting automobile tourism nationwide. 

Unlike other pictorial maps that emphasized interconnected highway systems, this state map was printed as a whimsical postcard, showcasing the state's diverse recreational resources and prominent industries.

views.title: The Maine Potato
views.interpretive_text: Misspelled “Aroostock” on the map. Aroostook County was once the nation’s largest producer of potatoes. Today, the Aroostook potato remains northern Maine’s primary agricultural product, producing 1.8 billion pounds of potatoes annually.

views.title: Maine's Industries
views.interpretive_text:
In addition to Maine’s well-known textile, paper, and timber industries, the map highlights lesser-known but significant enterprises, including shoe manufacturing, canoe building, and molybdenum mining. Molybdenum is a naturally occurring metallic element valued for its strength and resistance to heat and wear, making it an important component in industrial manufacturing, steel alloys, and modern electronics.

Maine’s shoemaking tradition dates to the Colonial era, when shoes were crafted by local artisans and small family businesses. During the Industrial Revolution, the growth of textile mills and factory production transformed the industry, enabling manufacturers to produce thousands of shoes each day.

views.title: State Symbols
views.interpretive_text: With brightly colored printing and memorable graphics, “Greetings From” postcards have entered our cultural history and scrapbooks. Among the state’s recreational activities and industries, the postcard also includes symbols for the state flag, the state floral emblem (white pine cone and tassel), and the state bird (chickadee).

title: Wabanaki Lands Today
short_description: How the political landscape has changed after 400 years of Euro-American Settlement.
credit:
Map of Maine lands held by Wabanaki tribes, 2026
Produced by the Maine Geospatial Library, Augusta, Maine

views.interpretive_text: Presented on a modern base map, the areas highlighted in purple are all the lands currently held by the four federally recognized tribes that reside in Maine. These different parcels have different designations such as reservation land, off reservation trust lands, property listed as assets by the tribal governments and lands help by native owned and directed non-profit organizations.

views.title: Two Passamaquoddy Communities
views.interpretive_text: The Passamaquoddy people have two distinct communities Downeast. Indian Township and Pleasant Point are the seats of the Passamaquoddy people in Maine.

views.title: Penobscot River Islands
views.interpretive_text: The Penobscot Nation’s territory includes thousands of acres of land, including more than 200 islands in the Penobscot River. The nation’s headquarters is located on Indian Island, adjacent to Old Town, Maine.

views.title: Native Lands in Northeastern Maine
views.interpretive_text: While they are two distinct Native nations, Micmacs and Maliseets living in Aroostook County joined together to form the Association of Aroostook Indians (AAI) in the mid 1960's. The two tribes went their separate ways and are now known as the Houlton Band of Maliseets and the Mi'kmaq Nation.  The history of their political partnership has led to the two nations having plots of land interspersed in northeastern Maine.

title: Maine Today
short_description: Get a closer look at Maine today!
credit:
Map of Maine, 2026
Produced by the Maine Geospatial Library, Augusta, Maine

views.interpretive_text: 400 years of colonization, boundary disputes, land divisions, expeditions, road and rail infrastructure and tourism shaped the Maine we have today. Today Maine is home to over 1.4 million people. It has industries in manufacturing, shipbuilding, agriculture, forestry, aquaculture and tourism, and is known for its rocky coast, dense forests, and scenic vistas.

views.title: Maine’s Unorganized Territory
views.interpretive_text:
Maine has several unorganized territories (UT), or areas which have no local incorporated municipal government. Maine’s UTs consist of 429 townships, which equal to slightly half the area of the entire State of Maine. These six-mile square blocks were created through several surveys in the 19th century. They are named through a range and number system and after specific land surveys. 

For example, T9 R8 WELS stands for Township 9, Range 8, West of the Eastern Line of the State.  The eastern line of the state refers to the straight north-south boundary line between Maine and Canada.

views.title: Maine's Public Lands
views.interpretive_text: Maine’s first state park was dedicated in 1938. However, public land acquisition was slow and by 1980, there were only around a dozen state parks, and two or three dozen wildlife management areas. The 1980s saw the sale of large tracts of forested land, which brought up concerns of land access and use. This awareness spurred the creation of several public and private programs, including the Land for Maine’s Future Program, established in 1987. This program, along with other purchases in the 1990s and 2000s, has increased Maine’s protected lands to 3.5 million acres, with 48 state parks and historic sites, 1 national park and 2 national monuments.
